FrMS88-de6700-d1e111.summary: Poses the nineteenth question: whether a sensitive or intellective power can naturally know a non-existent. Argument for: in Kings, Elisha's servant saw chariots and other things that were not there.
claims: Objection: Elisha's servant saw what did not exist.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e124.summary: Contrary: John, 'he who saw bore witness', which would not be valid if seeing could be false. First conclusion: the intellective power cannot intuitively know a non-existent. First proof: knowledge on which all our certainty depends cannot be false, since removing the first in an essential order removes the posterior; all our certainty depends on intuitive knowledge.
claims: The intellect cannot intuitively know a non-existent.
All the certainty of our knowledge depends on intuitive cognition.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e146.summary: Second proof: knowledge from which we argue to what is beyond doubt cannot be doubtful; from the intuitively known act of understanding we argue to what is beyond doubt in us, and we know we are certain.
claims: Intellective intuitive cognition cannot be doubtful.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e157.summary: Second conclusion: sensitive intuitive cognition cannot be false. First proof: no proposition with per se known truth can be false; sense truth apprehended intuitively is per se known, because terms are to principles as principles to conclusions, principles must be better known than conclusions, so terms better known than principles, and we know terms through the senses.
claims: Sensory intuitive cognition cannot be false.
Truths apprehended by intuitive sense are per se known.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e180.summary: Second proof: natural philosophy reaches its demonstrative conclusions only through the senses, so conclusions are no more certain than what the senses grasp; e.g. from seeing something moved we argue to an unmoved mover.
claims: Natural philosophy depends on the senses for its certainty.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e196.summary: Third proof: the most certain sciences presuppose nothing uncertain; metaphysics is most certain but presupposes knowledge of terms given through sense, so that knowledge is as certain as knowledge of principles.
claims: Metaphysical certainty presupposes certain sense knowledge of terms.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e207.summary: Confirms by the rule 'that because of which each thing is such is more so': we know principles because we know terms through sense, so we know the terms more.
claims: Terms known through sense are better known than principles.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e216.summary: Fourth proof: astronomy has demonstrations, which require terms obtained by sense, so sense truths are per se known. All these proofs share the force that the certain does not presuppose the uncertain. Then introduces experiments against this, the first from hearing: sound seems heard where it begins to be multiplied, but it propagates successively, so when it reaches the ear it no longer exists where it is heard, yet the hearing is true.
claims: The certain does not presuppose the uncertain.
Objection: sound is heard where it no longer exists.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e247.summary: Further experiments: the same odor pleases one and displeases another, so one perceives something non-existent; likewise taste (bitter to one, sweet to another), touch (one judges a thing hotter than another does), and the motion of a body between two fingers.
claims: Objection: contrary sensory judgments of the same object imply perception of the non-existent.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e263.summary: Explains, following Augustine (De Trinitate II), two modes of falsity: similarity (we cannot distinguish one thing from another and judge one to be the other) and conjunction (e.g. acts of phantasy and intellect are so joined we cannot tell them apart). Since the acts of the particular senses are similar to and conjoined with the act of the common sense, deception arises from inability to distinguish.
claims: Error arises from similarity and conjunction of acts.
Sensory deception arises from confusing the acts of the particular senses with that of the common sense.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e288.summary: First of four rules: the object alters the power both really and intentionally (as the sun the eye); intentional alteration is instantaneous, real alteration takes time, being motion and change.
claims: Objects alter sense powers intentionally in an instant and really over time.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e297.summary: Second rule: although particular senses apprehend common sensibles per se, they do not bear on them primarily; only the common sense does.
claims: Common sensibles are primarily the object of the common sense.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e304.summary: Third rule: phantasy judges differently when the object is present and moving a particular sense, conforming to it and judging the thing as it is, and when the object is absent.
claims: Phantasy judges correctly when conformed to a present object.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e313.summary: Fourth rule: a power accustomed to judge in one way continues to judge uniformly after the conditions change, unless the change is perceived — as someone used to rising facing east still judges so after the bed is turned.
claims: Habitual judgment persists after conditions change unless the change is noticed.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e326.summary: Reply to the sound experiment: one hears only the immediately present sound, suitably near the organ; the judgment that sound is where it began is the common sense's, which from the order of the present sound to the annihilated one still judges the first to be there; intentional alteration is instantaneous.
claims: One hears only the present, proximate sound; misplacement is the common sense's judgment.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e342.summary: Reply on pleasant and unpleasant: the judgment of these belongs to the common sense, not the particular sense, which apprehends precisely what is there.
claims: Hedonic judgments belong to the common sense.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e352.summary: Reply on bitterness: there is real bitterness, from a real admixture of a bitter humor.
claims: Perceived bitterness in illness is real, due to a bitter humor.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e359.summary: Reply on touch: the particular sense perceives heat, while the common sense judges intensity and remission.
claims: The common sense judges the intensity of heat.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e366.summary: Reply on motion: that judgment belongs to the common sense. Then raises difficult visual experiments, first Augustine's (De Trinitate I): after seeing a very bright body, bright colors appear afterwards.
claims: Judgments of motion belong to the common sense.
Objection: afterimages seem to show perception of the non-existent.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e379.summary: Reply: the object alters intentionally for the act of seeing, instantaneously and transiently, and really alters the spirits that carry species from place to place; these spirits receive true colors, which are seen after the first object departs.
claims: Afterimages are true colors received in the visual spirits.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e392.summary: Second experiment: varying colors on a dove's neck and on shot fabrics, said not to be really there; appeal to different parts fails, since the same part varies with the light. On Avicenna's view (perhaps defensible) the escape is easy: color exists actually only in the presence of light and is caused by light according to its approach, as a sunbeam through glass yields red, green, livid, and black at increasing distances.
claims: On Avicenna's view, colors exist actually only through light and vary with its approach.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e434.summary: Third experiment: paintings that appear to project in relief.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e440.summary: Reply: the common sense judges this, as shown by the fact that less practiced viewers judge so; it is not the particular sense.
claims: Illusions of relief belong to the common sense.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e447.summary: Fourth experiment, dreams: they are the work of imagination, which has abstractive cognition; or the external senses may not be entirely bound, so there is true sensation, as appears in those who argue or act in sleep as if awake.
claims: Dream images belong to imagination, which cognizes abstractively.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e460.summary: On demonic illusions: if produced in the external thing, they appear equally to all; if produced not in the object or medium but in the organ, the judgment and alteration are in the phantasy because the external senses are impeded.
claims: Demonic illusions operate either on the external object or on the phantasy.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e471.summary: On the mirror: the particular sense sees oneself, not an image, and is not deceived; the false judgment belongs to the common sense, which errs by the rule of habit, since sight is used to seeing in straight lines; the particular sense judges only color, the common sense judges location and distance.
claims: In mirror vision the particular sense is not deceived; the common sense misjudges location.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e493.summary: On the rainbow: there are true colors in it.
claims: The rainbow's colors are real.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e498.summary: On the whirled spark appearing as a circle: the common sense is deceived, judging continuity from the rapid succession of the spark's positions.
claims: The fiery circle is a misjudgment of the common sense due to rapid succession.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e510.summary: On trees and shore seeming to move to one on a ship: the common sense judges this; the particular sense sees only color and judges of it.
claims: Relative-motion illusions belong to the common sense.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e519.summary: On privation: privation is never sensed, so it must be denied that privation is seen.
claims: Privation is never sensed.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e524.summary: On the stick that appears broken in water: this is the interior common sense's erroneous judgment due to different alteration of sight through different transparent media.
claims: The bent-stick illusion is an error of the common sense caused by refraction.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e535.summary: On a broken mirror and a pressed eye producing doubling: sight does not perceive the duality; sight sees the object as it is, and the common sense judges duality.
claims: Double vision is a judgment of the common sense.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e546.summary: On seeing motion: an act of seeing lasts only an instant, so a new act occurs at each instant, as with a sunbeam; common sensibles like motion are grasped by the common sense, not the particular senses; motion, of which no part exists at once, is judged by the common sense alone, which is altered successively.
claims: Each act of seeing lasts an instant.
Motion is perceived by the common sense, not the particular senses.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e570.summary: On the moon: sight sees the moon, but the common sense judges its motion because of its varying distance from the clouds. Then examines the theory behind these experiments (attributed to Peter Auriol): the object is produced in apparent, seen, and cognized being. Meyronnes grants that in every apprehensive act the object is produced in some being, but argues that the being produced by vision presupposes another being in the object. First: a non-diminishing determination added to something does not vary it, and seen being is non-diminishing, else vision could destroy everything.
claims: The moon's apparent motion is a judgment of the common sense.
Every apprehensive act produces its object in some being, but seen being presupposes another being in the object.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e606.summary: Second: everything toward another is first in itself; seen being is toward another (the seer), so it presupposes some other being in the object.
claims: Seen being, as relational, presupposes absolute being in the object.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e615.summary: Third: producing in cognized being is simultaneous by nature with being produced; the act of seeing is naturally prior to producing, hence to being produced; but whenever the act exists it has a term; so in the prior instant the object has a term-being other than seen being.
claims: In the instant prior to its seen being, the object already terminates the act.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e635.summary: Fourth: all being secundum quid is founded on being simpliciter; seen being is secundum quid and founded in the object, so the object has some being simpliciter. Concludes that the object must have another being — not essential being, for then it would be known only abstractively, but actual existence.
claims: Seen being is founded on the object's actual existence, not merely its essential being.

FrMS88-de6700-d1e648.summary: Reply to the opening argument: Elisha's servant's seeing was a motion of the phantasy, to which perception of motion and such belongs.
claims: The servant's vision was an act of phantasy.

FrMS88-de6700.summary: The nineteenth question of the prologue asks whether a power, sensitive or intellective, can naturally know a non-existent intuitively. Meyronnes defends two conclusions: intellective intuitive cognition cannot be of a non-existent, since all the certitude of our knowledge depends on it and from intuited acts of understanding we argue to what is beyond doubt; and the intuitive cognition of the particular senses cannot be false, since sense truths furnish the terms of first principles and the premises of natural philosophy, metaphysics, and astronomy, and the certain cannot presuppose the uncertain. He then meets a long series of 'experiments' of sense illusion (sound heard where it begins, contrary judgments of smell, taste, and heat, the finger illusion, afterimages, the dove's neck and shot fabrics, raised paintings, dreams, demonic illusions, mirrors, the rainbow, the fiery circle of a whirled spark, apparently moving shores, privation, the bent stick in water, double vision, perception of motion, and the moon). Drawing on Augustine's two sources of error — similarity and conjunction — and four rules (real and intentional alteration; common sensibles judged by the common sense; phantasy's conformity when the object is present; habitual judgment persisting after a change), he assigns all such errors to the common sense or imagination, never to the particular sense, which grasps only what is there. Finally, against Peter Auriol's view that the object is produced in 'apparent' or 'seen' being, he concedes that every apprehensive act gives the object some being but argues that seen being presupposes another being in the object — not essence (which would make the cognition abstractive) but actual existence — since seen being is a non-diminishing, relational, secundum quid determination founded on being simpliciter. Elisha's servant's vision was a motion of phantasy.
claims: Intellective intuitive cognition cannot be of a non-existent, since all certainty depends on it.
The intuitive cognition of the particular senses cannot be false; sensory truths are per se known.
The certain cannot presuppose the uncertain, and all scientific certainty presupposes sense knowledge.
Sensory illusions arise in the common sense or imagination, not in the particular senses.
Error arises from similarity or conjunction of acts, as Augustine teaches.
The 'seen being' of an object presupposes its actual existence.
